messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When Minh Tran was 34, what began as several weeks of unexplained chest tightness and exhaustion turned into an emergency hospitalization for a severe cardiac infection that doctors told him could have killed him if he had come in later. He remembers the fluorescent brightness of the ICU, the rhythm of alarms that seemed to pause too long before someone appeared, and the helpless, watchful stretch of time while staff moved quickly around him without explaining much. What stayed with him most was the feeling that his body had become unpredictable and dangerous, as if something catastrophic had been developing inside him while he was still trying to work and act normal. Before that illness, Minh had thought of himself as competent, contained, the person who solved problems for clients and teammates as a UX designer. During the admission, dependent on machines and other people’s timing, he felt stripped of that identity.

In the months after discharge, he found that what had happened settled into a harsh judgment about himself. Minh had come to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him, not just medically but as a person. He spoke about “failing” at something as basic as staying healthy, and he was embarrassed by how frightened he had been in the hospital. The fear was quickly folded into a conviction that he was weak. When his wife tried to remind him that anyone would have been terrified after nearly dying, he dismissed it; to him, the fact that he still thought about the monitors and waiting meant he lacked some basic sturdiness other people had. Alongside this was a deadened quality he found hard to explain. He told the therapist he often felt “flat” or “not really there,” as though the illness had hollowed him out from the inside.

Those beliefs colored the way he now read danger. Because he felt his body had already betrayed him once and because he saw himself as weak and defective, small disruptions easily took on catastrophic meaning. If his physician’s office put him on hold too long, or if test results were not posted when expected, Minh was certain something bad was being withheld. A late email from a clinic could leave him pacing the apartment, muscles rigid, unable to settle. He no longer trusted reassurance. Even when his wife sat with him and pointed out that the cardiologist had said he was recovering well, he could not take in the idea of safety; it felt naïve, even reckless. His body stayed braced as if for another emergency, shoulders tight, jaw clenched, always scanning for the next sign that something was going wrong inside him.

Out of that sense of being weak and damaged, Minh began to organize his life around not having to face reminders of what had happened. He avoided thinking about the hospitalization and cut off conversations if his wife mentioned follow-up care or how scared they had both been. He delayed routine physical examinations and found reasons to reschedule appointments, telling himself he could not handle sitting in another waiting room and feeling exposed. Hospitals and ambulances had become especially potent; even passing the emergency entrance on the way to a client meeting made his chest tighten. He also started avoiding physical stress. Once an active cyclist, he gave up rides entirely because any increase in heart rate felt like proof that his body was fragile and that he was too weak to tolerate strain.

That vigilance then fed the avoidance further. In his daily work as a UX designer, delays are common—developers run behind, stakeholders reply late, prototypes take longer to load during presentations. Since the illness, each delay seems to hit his nervous system like a warning siren. When he waits longer than expected for a message from a doctor or even sees an ambulance idling outside his office building, his body goes rigid and his mind jumps immediately to disaster. To contain that surge, he closes browser tabs with the patient portal, skips appointments, and throws himself into tightly controlled work tasks that do not require him to think about his health. He has stopped joining coworkers for walks to get coffee because he worries the exertion will trigger something. These measures give brief relief, but they leave him more convinced that danger is everywhere and that he must stay on guard.

The same fear keeps reinforcing his view of himself. Each time he cannot tolerate a checkup, each time he needs his wife to look at a test notification because he cannot open it, Minh feels newly ashamed. His constant tension becomes evidence, in his own mind, that he is not recovering but revealing who he really is: a weak man with something wrong in him. The numbness has widened into his marriage; his wife experiences him as distant, and he knows he has become harder to reach. He is seeking help now after missing another follow-up appointment and spending the night awake, convinced the delay in rescheduling meant the clinic had seen something alarming in his chart. What frightens him most is that he may never again believe his body is safe, and what he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that he might learn how to live without feeling he is one delayed message away from catastrophe.
